Beneath most forests, the roots of trees are joined by threads of fungi known as mycorrhizae. The partnership itself is old and well documented: the fungus extends far beyond the reach of the roots, gathering water and minerals such as phosphorus, and in return the tree supplies the fungus with sugars made through photosynthesis. Because a single fungus can connect to several trees at once, and a single tree to several fungi, researchers began in the 1990s to describe forests as linked by shared underground networks. Some went further, proposing that large "mother trees" use these networks to send carbon to shaded seedlings and even to warn neighbors of insect attack.

These claims proved enormously popular, appearing in documentaries and best-selling books. Yet a number of forest ecologists have recently argued that the popular account has outrun the evidence. Their objection is not that the networks are imaginary; that fungi physically link trees has been shown repeatedly. The difficulty lies in what the links are said to do. In most field studies, carbon labeled with a traceable isotope moved from one tree to another only in very small amounts, and it was often unclear whether the carbon reached the second tree's tissues or remained inside the fungus. Moreover, many experiments could not rule out simpler routes, such as carbon leaking from roots into the soil and being absorbed by nearby roots without any fungal connection. Measurements were also usually taken over short periods, often a single growing season.

The critics also point out that the language of cooperation can mislead. A fungus that moves nutrients between trees may simply be serving its own interests, drawing resources from whichever partner offers the most. Describing this as a parent nurturing its offspring adds a moral story that the data do not require. None of this means that the original researchers were careless, or that further work will not confirm some of their bolder ideas. It means rather that a striking hypothesis became, in public discussion, a settled fact before the experiments needed to test it had been done.

Long before weather satellites, sailors kept careful records of the conditions they met at sea. Naval and merchant captains of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were required to note wind direction and strength, the state of the sky, and often the air temperature several times a day, chiefly so that a ship's position could be estimated when the coast was out of sight. A typical entry might record that the wind blew from the southwest as a moderate gale, that the sky was overcast with rain, and that the ship had covered a certain distance since noon. These logbooks, thousands of which survive in archives, were long treated as material for naval historians interested in voyages and battles. Over the past few decades, however, climate scientists have come to regard them as one of the richest sources of information about past weather over the oceans, which cover most of the planet but were otherwise almost unobserved.

Using the logbooks is not straightforward. Sailors described the wind in words rather than numbers, and the meaning of a term such as "fresh breeze" could differ between navies or change over time. Researchers have therefore compared the vocabulary of different fleets, matching each phrase to a likely range of wind speeds. They have also checked their translations against periods and places for which instrument readings exist. Where the descriptions of several ships sailing near one another agree, confidence in the reconstruction rises; where a single ship's record stands alone, it is used more cautiously.

The results have already proved useful. Reconstructions based on logbooks have helped show how the strength of major wind systems varied before the twentieth century, and they have provided a longer baseline against which recent changes can be measured. Some projects have enlisted volunteers to transcribe handwritten pages, since the material far exceeds what a few specialists could ever read. Perhaps as notable is the shift in how the documents themselves are viewed. Records created for one practical purpose, navigation, have turned out to answer questions their authors could not have imagined, a reminder that the value of an archive is not fixed by the intentions of those who produced it.

For a long time, textbooks told a simple story about the arrival of oil painting in Europe. Painters in Italy and elsewhere, the story went, worked in egg tempera, a quick-drying paint made by mixing pigment with egg yolk, until a few artists in the Low Countries invented oil paint early in the fifteenth century. The new medium was said to have spread rapidly southward, and within a generation tempera had been abandoned. The story was attractive because it gave the change a clear starting point and a small set of heroes.

Technical study of the paintings themselves has complicated this account. When conservators examine tiny samples of paint under the microscope or analyze them chemically, they often find that drying oils were used long before the fifteenth century, in decorative work and sometimes in panel paintings. They also find that many works once described as pure tempera or pure oil are in fact mixtures: a painter might lay in the lower layers in tempera and then add glazes of oil on top, or blend the two binders within a single layer. What the Netherlandish painters achieved, it now appears, was not the invention of a material but the refinement of a method, a way of building up thin, translucent layers that gave colors unusual depth and allowed extremely fine detail.

The shift away from tempera was therefore gradual and uneven. Some workshops adopted oil for certain parts of a picture, such as the deep shadows of drapery, while keeping tempera for flesh tones, which painters were used to handling in small, precise strokes. Local habits, the cost of materials and the expectations of patrons all affected the pace of change, so that one city might embrace the new method decades before its neighbor. Such findings do not diminish the achievement of the early masters, whose work remains remarkable. They do suggest, however, that changes in artistic technique are rarely the work of one moment, and that the evidence held in the paintings can correct histories written mostly from documents and reputation.

Most planetary scientists believe that the Moon formed after a body roughly the size of Mars struck the young Earth about four and a half billion years ago. According to this giant-impact hypothesis, the collision threw a vast quantity of vaporized and molten rock into orbit, where it gradually gathered into the Moon. The hypothesis replaced several older ideas. One held that the Moon had split off from a rapidly spinning Earth; another, that it had formed elsewhere and been captured by Earth's gravity; a third, that Earth and Moon had formed side by side from the same cloud of material.

The giant-impact hypothesis won acceptance largely because it explained facts the others could not. Rock samples returned by the Apollo missions indicated that the Moon has very little iron at its center compared with Earth, which fits a scenario in which the Moon formed mostly from the outer, rocky layers of the colliding bodies rather than from their iron cores. The samples also showed that lunar rocks contain almost no water or other substances that evaporate easily, as would be expected if the material had been intensely heated. And computer models showed that an off-center collision could give the Earth-Moon system the large amount of spin it has today.

Yet one finding has proved stubborn. In most simulations, the bulk of the Moon comes from the impacting body, not from Earth. Since bodies that formed in different parts of the solar system usually differ in the proportions of certain isotopes, the Moon ought to differ chemically from Earth. Instead, careful measurements show that the isotopic makeup of lunar and terrestrial rocks is nearly identical. Researchers have responded in several ways: some propose that the impactor happened to resemble Earth closely, others that the collision was so violent that the material of both bodies was thoroughly mixed. None of these proposals has yet won general agreement, but few scientists regard the puzzle as a reason to abandon the hypothesis itself. Instead, it has become a test that any detailed version of the hypothesis must pass.

Economists long assumed that people saving for retirement weigh costs and benefits and choose accordingly. If this were true, the way a choice is presented should matter little: a worker who wants to save will join a savings plan whether joining requires filling out a form or happens automatically. Studies of workplace pension plans have challenged this assumption. When companies switched from plans that employees had to opt into to plans in which employees were enrolled unless they chose to leave, participation rose sharply, in some cases from under half of new workers to nearly all of them. Because the plans were otherwise unchanged, offering the same investments and the same contributions from the employer, the difference could not be explained by better terms.

Several explanations have been offered. One emphasizes inertia: deciding how much to save and where to invest it is tedious, and many people put off unpleasant decisions indefinitely, so whatever happens when they do nothing tends to persist. Another holds that people read the default as advice, assuming that the employer, who presumably understands the plan, has chosen a sensible option for them. A third points to loss aversion, the tendency to feel a loss more keenly than an equal gain: once money is already being set aside, stopping the contributions feels like giving something up.

The findings have led many governments and firms to adopt automatic enrollment, but they also raise questions. A default influences people who have no strong view, and it therefore also influences those for whom it is poorly suited. A worker carrying expensive debt, for instance, might be better off paying it down than saving at the default rate. Moreover, studies have found that many automatically enrolled workers stay at the initial contribution rate for years, even when it is lower than the rate they would have chosen on their own. Defaults, in other words, do not simply help people do what they already intend; they shape what people end up doing. Designing them well thus requires a judgment about which outcome suits most people, a judgment that can no longer be left entirely to each individual.

Many of the best-known English novels of the nineteenth century first reached readers not as complete books but in installments. A novel might appear in monthly parts, each a few chapters long and sold separately for a modest price, or in weekly portions printed in a magazine alongside other material. A single story could take a year and a half or more to finish, and readers who began it in the spring might not learn its ending until the autumn of the following year. The low price of each part also brought novels within reach of many readers who could never have afforded a complete book in several volumes.

This manner of publication left clear marks on the novels themselves. Because each part had to hold the attention of readers who might otherwise stop buying, authors tended to close installments at moments of suspense or unresolved conflict. Large casts of characters and multiple plot lines, which allowed a writer to move between stories from one part to the next, became common. Authors also wrote while earlier parts were already in print, so they could not revise the opening once they knew how the story would end. Some took advantage of this situation, responding to letters from readers or to sales figures by enlarging a popular character's role or changing a planned outcome.

For much of the twentieth century, critics tended to treat these features as flaws, the price an author paid for writing under commercial pressure. More recent scholars have been less dismissive. They point out that serial readers experienced a novel over many months, discussing each part with friends and family and speculating about what would come next, so that the story became a shared event in a way that a single volume rarely is. Seen in this light, the loose structure and frequent suspense were not merely concessions to the market; they were suited to a particular way of reading, one in which a long pause between chapters was part of the pleasure rather than an interruption of it.

Across northern Europe and North America, travelers have long noticed large boulders sitting alone in fields and forests, often made of a kind of rock found nowhere nearby. Some of these stones weigh hundreds of tons, and a few rest on ledges or hilltops where no river could have carried them. Geologists call them erratics, from a Latin word meaning "wandering," and for much of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries their presence was one of the most puzzling problems in the study of the earth.

The most widely accepted explanation at first was that the boulders had been moved by a great flood. Water, the reasoning went, could carry enormous loads if it moved fast enough, and a flood of sufficient size might have swept stones across whole regions. A later version of this idea proposed that the boulders had been frozen into icebergs that drifted over a sea once covering the land and dropped their loads as they melted. This "drift" theory had real strengths: icebergs do carry rocks, and sailors had seen them do so. Its weakness was that it required the sea to have covered vast areas, including high ground, for which other evidence was scarce.

The explanation that eventually prevailed came from people who knew mountain glaciers well. In the Alps, observers noted that living glaciers carry rock on and within the ice, polish and scratch the bedrock beneath them, and leave ridges of debris where they stop. Similar scratches and ridges could be found far from any present glacier, often lined up in the same direction as the trail of erratics. The conclusion, startling at the time, was that sheets of ice far larger than any Alpine glacier had once covered much of the northern continents. It took decades for this idea to win wide acceptance, partly because the scale it demanded seemed incredible. Yet its success rested on a sound method: it explained a puzzling feature of the landscape by a process that could be observed at work in the present, merely on a larger scale. The older theories were not foolish; they too appealed to known forces. What they lacked was the detailed match between cause and evidence that the scratched rock provided.

Sociologists who study city life have long distinguished between the home, the workplace and a third kind of setting: the cafés, barbershops, libraries and small parks where people gather without being required to. Such "third places," as they are sometimes called, have several features in common. They are inexpensive or free to enter, they are open for long hours, and they are used by a mix of regulars and newcomers. Conversation in them is usually informal, and no one is expected to stay for any particular length of time. Unlike a club, a third place asks for no membership, and unlike a shop in a shopping mall, it does not hurry its visitors along.

Researchers have argued that these places matter more than their modest appearance suggests. In surveys, residents of neighborhoods with many such gathering spots report knowing more of their neighbors by name and are more likely to say they could ask a neighbor for help. One explanation is simple repetition: seeing the same faces week after week turns strangers into acquaintances, and acquaintances sometimes into friends. Another is that third places mix people who would otherwise rarely meet, since a café counter or a library table brings together people of different ages and occupations. Studies have also found that local businesses of this kind often serve as informal message boards, where news of jobs, rooms to rent and community events passes from person to person.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that simply building more cafés will strengthen a neighborhood. The surveys show that the two things go together, but not which causes which. People who already have close ties to their neighbors may be the ones who support local gathering places, keeping them in business. In that case the cafés would be a sign of a close community rather than its source. Moreover, the features that make a place welcoming are hard to plan: an owner who remembers customers' names, a room where lingering is not discouraged, prices that do not exclude long-time residents. Planners who hope to encourage community life may therefore do better by protecting the places that already serve this role than by designing new ones from scratch.

Musicians today generally tune to a standard in which the A above middle C vibrates 440 times per second. It is easy to assume that some such standard has always existed, but for most of the history of Western music it did not. Pitch varied from city to city and even from building to building. A church organ, which could not easily be retuned, set the pitch for the singers and instrumentalists who performed with it, and organs built in different places and periods could differ by more than a semitone. A piece sung comfortably in one town might strain the voices of a choir in the next.

For much of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries this variety caused only occasional trouble, but as musicians traveled more and orchestras began to use instruments made by distant manufacturers, the inconvenience grew. A further problem was that pitch tended to rise. Instrument makers and players found that a slightly higher tuning made an orchestra sound brighter and more brilliant, and each small increase was hard to reverse once instruments had been built for it. Singers complained that music written for earlier generations had become harder to perform, since the same written notes now lay higher in their voices.

Efforts to fix a standard therefore came partly from singers and composers who wished to halt the upward drift. In the mid-nineteenth century one national government established an official pitch somewhat lower than the one then common in many orchestras, and several other countries followed its lead. The figure of 440 was agreed at an international conference in the twentieth century, aided by new electronic devices that could produce a precise tone and transmit it by radio. Even now the standard is not universal: some orchestras tune slightly higher, and many performers of early music deliberately use lower pitches that they believe are closer to those the composers knew. The history of pitch thus shows that a seemingly natural fact of music is in large part the product of practical needs, technical change and negotiation.

Sleep poses a puzzle for biologists. An animal that sleeps cannot look for food, find a mate or watch for predators, and yet nearly every animal that has been carefully studied, from fruit flies to whales, sleeps in some form. Even animals that live in constant danger, such as small grazing mammals, spend a substantial part of each day asleep, and laboratory animals kept from sleeping for long periods soon show signs of poor health. The persistence of sleep across so many species suggests that it serves functions important enough to outweigh its dangers, functions that researchers believe include the repair of tissues and the strengthening of memories.

Some animals have found a way to reduce the cost. Dolphins and many other marine mammals can sleep with one half of the brain at a time. Recordings of their brain activity show that while one hemisphere displays the slow waves typical of deep sleep, the other remains awake, and the eye connected to the waking hemisphere often stays open. This arrangement allows a dolphin to keep swimming and to rise to the surface to breathe, which it must do consciously, while still obtaining the rest it needs. Certain birds show a similar ability: ducks resting in a row have been observed keeping open the eye that faces away from the group, as if guarding the flank.

Studies of birds that migrate over the ocean have extended these findings in an unexpected direction. Using small devices that record brain activity, researchers found that frigatebirds, which can stay aloft for weeks at a time, sleep in flight. Most of this sleep takes place in one hemisphere at a time, but some occurs in both hemispheres at once, and it amounts to less than an hour a day, far less than the same birds sleep on land. Such results suggest that the amount of sleep an animal takes is not fixed by its biology alone but can be adjusted to its circumstances. They also raise the question of how the birds manage on so little, a question whose answer may eventually shed light on the functions of sleep itself.

For most of the twentieth century, loading and unloading a cargo ship was slow, costly work. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every size, and teams of laborers moved them piece by piece into the ship's hold, where they had to be fitted together so that the load would not shift at sea. A ship might spend as long in port as it did at sea, and theft and damage were common. Economists estimated that handling at the ports often made up a large share of the total cost of shipping goods overseas.

The standardized shipping container changed this. Goods packed into large steel boxes of uniform size at a factory could be moved by truck or train to a port, lifted onto a ship by crane, and unloaded at the other end without anyone touching the contents. Ships designed for containers could be loaded in hours rather than days. Because the boxes were the same everywhere, the cranes, trucks, rail cars and ships of different companies and countries could all handle them, and the savings grew as more of the world adopted the system.

Historians of trade have debated how much of the growth of world commerce since the 1960s the container deserves credit for. Some early accounts gave it a central place, but others argued that trade agreements and falling tariffs were more important. Recent statistical studies suggest that the container's effect was large but appeared gradually, since its full benefits depended on ports, railways and roads being rebuilt to handle it, a process that took decades in many countries. The container also had consequences beyond trade itself. Ports that could not accommodate large container ships declined, while new ones arose on open land beside deep water, and the dockside neighborhoods that had depended on large numbers of laborers changed sharply. The story of the container is thus a reminder that an apparently simple invention can depend on, and in turn reshape, a great deal of surrounding infrastructure.

In the hot, dry regions of the Middle East and South Asia, many older houses are topped by tall towers with openings near the top. These wind-catchers, as they are often called, were built centuries before electric fans or air conditioning, and they could keep the rooms beneath them noticeably cooler than the air outside. Visitors have sometimes described them as picturesque relics, but engineers who have studied them have come to see them as sophisticated devices that exploit several physical effects at once. A single tower, in this view, is less a decoration than a carefully tuned machine with no moving parts, refined over generations of trial and error by local builders.

The most obvious effect is the capture of wind. Air moving across the top of the tower is directed down a shaft into the house, where it flows over the occupants and carries away heat. Because wind near the ground is slowed by buildings and trees, a tall tower reaches faster, cleaner air than a window could. Many towers also work when the air is still. During the day the shaft walls, built of thick masonry, absorb heat slowly; at night they release it, warming the air inside the shaft so that it rises and draws cooler air through the rooms below. In some designs the incoming air passes over a pool or an underground water channel, and the evaporation of water cools it further.

Researchers have measured temperature differences of several degrees between the rooms served by a wind-catcher and the outside air, though results depend heavily on the weather, the orientation of the tower and the layout of the house. Architects interested in reducing the energy used by buildings have begun to borrow the principle, designing modern towers with adjustable vents and sensors. They do not expect such towers to replace mechanical cooling in the hottest climates. But they argue that a structure using only wind, heat and water can reduce how much mechanical cooling a building needs, and that the old towers show how much careful design can accomplish without any machinery at all.

For much of the twentieth century, psychologists tended to picture long-term memory as a kind of storehouse. An experience, once it had been consolidated into lasting form, was thought to remain more or less fixed, fading perhaps with time but not otherwise changing. Recalling a memory, on this view, was like taking a book from a shelf: the act of reading did not alter the text.

Research over the past few decades has challenged that picture. In one well-known line of experiments, people watched a film of a traffic accident and were later asked questions about it. When the questions were worded to suggest a detail that had not appeared in the film, such as broken glass, many participants later reported remembering it. Other studies found that people who repeatedly imagined a childhood event that had never occurred sometimes came to believe that it had. Work with animals pointed in the same direction: when a stored memory was recalled, it seemed to become briefly unstable, and drugs given during that window could weaken it. Such findings suggest that remembering is partly an act of reconstruction. Each time a memory is retrieved, it may be stored again in a slightly altered form, absorbing information from the present.

These results have practical consequences, especially for legal systems that rely on the testimony of witnesses. A witness who is shown a suspect's photograph, or who hears other witnesses discuss an event, may sincerely remember things differently afterward. Confidence is not a reliable guide either, since a memory can grow more certain each time it is repeated even as it drifts from what happened. Many researchers now recommend that police record a witness's first account promptly and avoid suggestive questions.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that memory is generally untrustworthy. Most memories of ordinary events are broadly accurate, and the errors studied in the laboratory usually concern details rather than the main outline of an experience. The lesson is not that people should doubt everything they remember, but that memory is an active process, and that the conditions under which it is recalled deserve as much care as the conditions under which it was formed.

Many concrete structures built today are expected to last perhaps fifty to a hundred years before they need major repair. Yet some structures built by the Romans two thousand years ago, including harbor walls that have stood in seawater for centuries, remain in remarkably good condition. For a long time, the durability of Roman concrete was attributed mainly to its ingredients, particularly the volcanic ash that Roman builders mixed with lime. This ash reacts with lime and water to form compounds that bind the material firmly together.

More recent studies have added a surprising detail. Roman concrete often contains small white lumps of lime, a few millimeters across, scattered through the material. These lumps had usually been dismissed as evidence of careless mixing or poor-quality ingredients. Researchers who examined them closely, however, found that they may have been produced deliberately, by mixing the lime into the concrete while it was still hot from processing rather than first combining it with water. More important, the lumps appear to give the concrete a capacity to repair itself. When a crack forms and water seeps in, the water dissolves some of the lime in a nearby lump, and the dissolved lime then reacts to form new mineral crystals that can fill the crack before it spreads.

In seawater structures, a further process seems to be at work. Water passing through the concrete reacts with the volcanic ash to grow mineral crystals within the material over time, strengthening it rather than wearing it down. Modern concrete, by contrast, is designed to be as stable as possible once it has set, and chemical reactions that continue inside it are usually a sign of damage.

Engineers are now testing mixtures that copy some of these features, partly in the hope of producing concrete that lasts longer and needs less frequent replacement. They caution, however, that Roman concrete was weaker than modern concrete under heavy loads and took longer to set, so it could not simply replace current materials in tall buildings or bridges. The aim is rather to borrow particular ideas, such as self-healing, from a material whose qualities were long misunderstood.

Archaeologists reconstructing what ancient peoples ate have traditionally relied on the remains that survive best: animal bones, shells, and the charred seeds of plants. Because bones last far longer than soft plant tissue, this evidence has tended to give an impression of diets dominated by meat, especially for periods before the beginnings of farming. Plant foods such as roots, tubers and wild grasses were almost certainly eaten, but they rarely left a visible trace.

A newer technique has begun to correct this imbalance. Plants store energy in tiny granules of starch, and these granules can become trapped in the cracks and pores of stone tools used to grind or pound plant material. Under the right conditions they survive for tens of thousands of years. Because the granules of different plants vary in size and shape, a trained researcher examining them under a microscope can often identify the plant family, and sometimes the species, that a tool was used to process. Some granules also show signs of swelling or damage that indicate the food was cooked.

Studies using this method have found starch from wild cereals and tubers on grinding stones far older than the earliest farming settlements. The results suggest that some groups were collecting and preparing plant foods intensively long before they began to cultivate them, and that the shift to agriculture may have built on an existing familiarity with such plants rather than beginning from nothing.

The technique has limits. Starch can enter a tool from the soil in which it was buried, so careful researchers compare samples from the tool with samples from the surrounding sediment. Some plants produce granules that are difficult to tell apart. And a tool with starch on it shows that a plant was processed, not how large a part of the diet it made up. Used with these cautions, however, the method gives archaeologists access to a part of the ancient diet that was long invisible to them, and it has already made the picture of early human eating noticeably more varied.

For most of history, units of measurement were local and varied. A foot or a pound in one region might differ noticeably from the unit of the same name a few days' travel away, which complicated trade and made it hard to compare the results of scientific work. In the late eighteenth century, French scientists proposed a new system meant to be universal. Its unit of length, the meter, was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along a line passing through Paris, so that anyone, anywhere, could in principle reconstruct it from the size of the earth itself.

In practice, the definition depended on an object. After surveyors spent years measuring part of that line, a bar of platinum was made to the calculated length and kept in an archive, and later a more durable bar of platinum and iridium served as the international standard. Copies were distributed to many countries and periodically compared with the original. This arrangement worked well enough for ordinary purposes, but it had obvious weaknesses. A bar can be damaged or lost, its length changes slightly with temperature, and comparisons with it can be made only where it is kept.

In the twentieth century, scientists moved toward definitions based on constants of nature. The meter was first defined by the wavelength of light given off by a particular kind of atom, and later, in 1983, by the distance light travels in a vacuum in a specific tiny fraction of a second. Because the speed of light is the same everywhere, any well-equipped laboratory can now realize the meter without reference to a stored object. Other units have since followed the same path, and the last standard kept as a physical object was retired in 2019. In a sense this fulfilled the original ambition of the eighteenth-century reformers, though by means they could not have foreseen: the unit is once again tied to nature rather than to an artifact, but to a property of light rather than to the dimensions of the planet.

Double-entry bookkeeping, in which every transaction is recorded twice, once as a debit in one account and once as a credit in another, is today so common that it is easy to overlook how unusual it once was. The method appears in the account books of merchants in several Italian cities by the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century, and it was described in print in a widely read mathematics textbook in 1494. Over the following centuries it spread across Europe and eventually throughout the world.

Historians have offered different accounts of why the method mattered. One influential argument held that double entry was essential to the rise of modern capitalism. By forcing merchants to treat their business as a unit separate from their household and to calculate profit systematically, the argument went, the method encouraged a rational, profit-seeking outlook that made large-scale enterprise possible. On this view, a technique of record keeping helped to shape a whole economic mentality.

Later historians have been more cautious. Studies of surviving account books show that many merchants who used double entry did not regularly calculate overall profit at all; they used their books chiefly to keep track of what others owed them and what they owed in turn. Other merchants ran perfectly successful businesses with simpler single-entry records for generations. Moreover, some of the great trading companies of the seventeenth century did not adopt double entry promptly, suggesting that it was not a precondition for enterprise on a large scale.

Yet the method's appeal is not hard to understand. Because each entry has a matching counterpart, the two sides of the books should always balance, and a failure to balance signals an error somewhere. This built-in check made the records more trustworthy, both to the merchant and to partners, lenders and courts who might need to examine them. Its importance may therefore lie less in transforming how merchants thought than in making their dealings easier to verify: a more modest role, but not a small one.

The algae use sunlight to make sugars, a large share of which they pass to the coral; the coral in turn gives the algae shelter and access to nutrients. When water becomes unusually warm, this partnership can break down. The algae become damaged and are expelled, the coral loses its color, and it is said to have bleached. Such events can affect large stretches of a reef at once, turning wide areas pale within a few weeks. A bleached coral is not dead, and it can recover if conditions improve quickly, but if the stress continues it may starve.

For many years the algae living in corals were treated as more or less a single kind. Genetic studies have since shown that they belong to many distinct types, which differ in how well they tolerate heat. Some corals host several types at once, and the mixture can change. After a period of stress, a coral may emerge with a larger proportion of heat-tolerant algae than before, a process researchers sometimes call shuffling. The change seems to happen in two ways: algae already present in small numbers may multiply, or the coral may take up new algae from the surrounding water. Corals that have shuffled in this way have, in some studies, bleached less severely during the next warm period.

This discovery has attracted interest because it suggests that corals have a way to adjust to warmer water faster than evolution through changes in the coral's own genes would allow. Researchers caution, however, that the benefit has costs and limits. Heat-tolerant algae often supply less sugar to their hosts, so corals that rely on them may grow more slowly and reproduce less. Not every coral species can take up new types of algae, and some appear to keep the same partners throughout their lives. And the gain in heat tolerance observed so far amounts to roughly one or two degrees, which may help corals through occasional warm spells without protecting them from larger, lasting changes.

When synchronized sound arrived in the late 1920s, many observers predicted that it would ruin the art of film. Silent cinema had developed a rich visual language: performers conveyed emotion through gesture and facial expression, and directors told stories through the arrangement of images, with only occasional printed titles to supply dialogue. Critics feared that recorded speech would turn films into mere photographs of stage plays, in which characters stood still and talked.

In the short term, some of these fears were justified. Early sound equipment was cumbersome. Microphones picked up only what was close to them, so actors had to stay near hidden microphones, and noisy cameras were enclosed in soundproof booths that made them hard to move. Films of the first few sound years are often noticeably static, with long scenes of conversation shot from a fixed position. Some performers whose style had depended on broad gesture seemed exaggerated once audiences could hear them speak, and acting moved toward a quieter, more conversational manner.

Within a few years, however, technical improvements restored much of the lost freedom. Microphones were mounted on movable poles, cameras were made quieter, and sound could be recorded separately and combined with the image afterward. Directors discovered that sound could do more than reproduce speech. Off-screen noises could suggest a space larger than the frame showed; a sudden silence could create tension; music could tell viewers how to feel about an image before anything happened in it.

Looking back, film historians tend to describe the coming of sound less as a loss than as a transformation. Something real was given up: the particular expressive style of the silent performer did not survive, and some admired careers ended. But the medium that emerged was not simply silent film with talking added. It combined image and sound in ways that neither the stage nor the silent screen had allowed, which is why the early predictions now seem to have mistaken a temporary limitation for a permanent one.

Anyone who has kept a plant on a windowsill has seen it bend toward the light. In the late nineteenth century, Charles Darwin and his son Francis investigated this habit using young grass seedlings, whose first shoot is enclosed in a slender protective sheath. When they lit the seedlings from one side, the shoots curved toward the light, with the bending taking place in a region somewhat below the tip. Yet when the Darwins covered the very tip with a small cap that blocked light, the shoots did not bend, even though the region that normally curved was left exposed. Covering the lower region instead, while leaving the tip uncovered, did not prevent bending.

From these results the Darwins concluded that the tip senses the light and that some influence must travel from the tip down to the region where bending occurs. They could not say what this influence was. Over the following decades, other researchers took up the question. One showed that the influence could pass across a thin layer of gelatin placed between a cut tip and the rest of the shoot, but not across a sheet of material that blocked chemicals, suggesting that the signal was a substance rather than, say, an electrical impulse. Another found that a cut tip placed on one side of a shoot whose own tip had been removed caused it to curve away from that side, even in darkness.

The substance was eventually identified as one of a group of plant hormones now called auxins. When a shoot is lit from one side, auxin collects on the shaded side, where it causes cells to lengthen more than those on the lit side, and the uneven growth curves the shoot toward the light. The story is often told as a model of how scientific understanding grows: a careful observation, a simple experiment that rules out one explanation, and a series of later studies, each designed to answer a question the previous one had left open.

Using tools was once considered one of the clearest marks separating humans from other animals. That view has long since been abandoned: chimpanzees strip twigs to fish for termites, sea otters crack shellfish on stones, and some birds use sticks to probe for insects. Among the most striking cases are the crows of New Caledonia, an island group in the southwest Pacific. These birds not only use tools but make them, shaping twigs into hooks and cutting the stiff edges of leaves into barbed probes that they use to pull grubs from holes in dead wood.

What makes the crows especially interesting to researchers is the question of how they acquire this skill. Young crows raised in captivity without ever seeing an adult use a tool will still pick up sticks and poke them into crevices, which suggests that some tendency toward tool use is inherited. Yet their early attempts are clumsy, and wild juveniles spend a long time near their parents, often handling tools the adults have dropped. Researchers have also found that the shapes of leaf tools differ from one area of the islands to another, and that these local styles have remained stable over many years. One explanation is that young birds learn the local design by watching and copying, so that a style can be passed on from one generation to the next.

Some writers have been quick to describe these local styles as a form of culture. Many researchers prefer caution. Differences between areas might reflect differences in the plants available rather than learned traditions, and experiments that could separate the two explanations are difficult to carry out in the wild. Still, the crows show that the capacities involved in making tools, including inherited tendencies, practice and possibly social learning, can arise in animals whose brains are organized very differently from those of primates. Studying them may therefore help researchers understand which ingredients of tool use are truly necessary, and which are simply the ones that happened to appear in our own lineage.

In the nineteenth century, many of Europe's medieval churches and castles were in poor repair, and an energetic movement arose to restore them. Its leading figures believed that a restorer should return a building to the condition its original designers had intended, or even to the ideal form it would have taken had they been able to complete it. Following this principle, architects removed later additions they considered out of keeping, rebuilt missing towers and replaced worn carvings with new ones in what they judged to be the correct style. In some cases they replaced sound medieval work simply because it did not match their idea of what the building should have been. Their work was often skillful, and some of it rested on careful study of surviving buildings of the period.

The movement soon provoked fierce opposition. Its critics argued that the restorers were not recovering the past but inventing it. A medieval building, they pointed out, was rarely the product of a single plan; it had been altered over centuries, and those alterations were themselves part of its history. To strip them away in the name of an original design was to replace a genuine record with a modern guess. Restoration of this kind, one critic suggested, was like repainting an old portrait so that its sitter looked younger: the result might be handsome, but it was no longer a faithful likeness. The critics urged instead that old buildings be protected and repaired as needed but not remade, so that what survived would remain authentic, even if incomplete.

The principle the critics championed eventually prevailed, and international guidelines for the care of monuments now generally discourage reconstruction based on conjecture. Yet the principle is harder to apply than to state. Every repair involves some replacement of material, and the line between necessary repair and creative restoration is not always clear. Moreover, the restorations of the nineteenth century have themselves become historical. Many visitors admire buildings whose most famous features are largely nineteenth-century work, and removing those features now would be to commit, in reverse, the very error the critics condemned.

Few questions in economic history have been argued as long or as fiercely as whether the early decades of industrialization in Britain made ordinary workers better or worse off. The so-called pessimists, drawing on contemporary descriptions of crowded towns and long factory hours, held that the material condition of laborers stagnated or declined between roughly 1780 and 1840. The optimists countered with series of wages and prices suggesting that real earnings, after a slow start, had begun to rise well before the middle of the nineteenth century. For a time the debate seemed to turn on which collection of numbers was the more trustworthy.

That framing, however, obscured how much the answer depends on what is being measured. Wage series typically record the daily rate paid to adult men in particular trades; they say little about how many days a year such men actually found work, or about the earnings of women and children, whose contributions to household income were often substantial and whose employment shifted markedly during the period. Price indices pose comparable problems, since the goods a working family bought, and the proportions in which it bought them, are reconstructed largely by inference. Small differences in such assumptions can turn a modest gain into a modest loss.

More recent work has sought to sidestep these difficulties by turning to measures not denominated in money at all. Records of the heights of soldiers and convicts, for instance, have been used as an index of childhood nutrition and health, on the reasoning that a population that is poorly fed or frequently ill in youth grows up shorter. Several such studies find that average heights fell for cohorts born in the early nineteenth century, even as most wage series edged upward. This apparent paradox need not mean that either kind of evidence is mistaken. Rising money incomes can coexist with deteriorating welfare if, for example, workers moved to towns where wages were higher but sanitation was worse and food more expensive.

The upshot is not that the original question was meaningless, but that it was underspecified. "Better off" bundles together income, health, security and the conditions of work, and there is no compelling reason to expect these to have moved in tandem. To insist on a single verdict is to presuppose a commensurability among them that the evidence itself calls into question.
